question: Did foreign money build India? What 56 years of FDI data show.

theme.label: Economy and public money
readerQuestions: What is the headline economic number?
Is this a total number or a per-person number?
How much of the story is prices, exchange rates, or GDP share?
What does this explain about household life?

plannedCharts.title: How much of what India builds is paid for by foreigners
plannedCharts.unit: percent of gross fixed capital formation
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The whole article in one line: FDI has never financed more than about a tenth of Indian capital formation.

plannedCharts.title: Fifty-six years, and India is almost always the bottom line
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: World Bank data starts in 1970 and covers the closed decades UNCTAD's series cannot reach.

plannedCharts.title: India did climb, and the climb was real
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The success story is genuine and has to be told before it is qualified.

plannedCharts.title: Two different ways to build a country
plannedCharts.unit: percent of gross fixed capital formation
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The FDI-led model and the domestic-capital model, on one axis.

plannedCharts.title: India is the South Asian norm, not the exception
plannedCharts.unit: percent of gross fixed capital formation
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The obvious objection is that a low share is an Indian failure. The neighbours say it is a regional pattern.

plannedCharts.title: Thirty-six years of foreign investment, per Indian
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Scale intuition: India's total is large only because India is large.

plannedCharts.title: Where the factories actually went
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The China-plus-one reallocation is the central economic event of the last decade, and the data says where it landed.

plannedCharts.title: India's slice of the developing world's investment
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The share tells you whether India is gaining ground on its actual competitors, not on the world.

plannedCharts.title: How much of the economy foreigners actually own
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Flows are noisy; the accumulated stock is what decades of policy actually produced.

plannedCharts.title: Building something new, or buying something old
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Foreign money either builds new capacity or changes the nameplate on capacity that already exists. Only one of those adds to capital formation.

plannedCharts.title: What gets announced, and what turns up

series.label: FDI recorded in the balance of payments

plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India announced a record project pipeline in the same year it booked its smallest inflow in a decade.

plannedCharts.title: India's FDI, era by era
plannedCharts.unit: US$ billion received over the period
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Five distinct policy eras, and the best one is not the most recent.

plannedCharts.title: Indian firms announce projects abroad too
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The maturity story shows up in announced projects as well as in the accumulated stock.

plannedCharts.title: Two stakes converging
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The closing gap is the sign of a maturing economy, not a crisis, and it is where this article hands off.

plannedCharts.title: Where the developing world's biggest firms come from
plannedCharts.unit: number of firms in the top 100
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A country that does not build multinationals stays a destination for other people's capital rather than a source of its own.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
